text: I'm going to get an update from the Chancellor on Grangemouth in just a minute. He's clearly not interested in Grangemouth. You would have thought on a day like this that he'd want to welcome the 120 million pounds of investment into Grangemouth. It's a landmark investment, protecting 500 jobs and hundreds more across Scotland's supply chain, and he can't even bring himself to mention it. Mr. Speaker, that's on top of the Typhoon defense jobs in Edinburgh and shipbuilding jobs on the Clyde. And after decades of SNP rule, they're totally out of ideas. They can't even welcome the Grangemouth news. Scotland deserves change next year with Anas Sarwar.

Can I send, I'm sure, condolences of the whole house to Andrew's family. It's an awful case and every life that's lost to dangerous driving is a tragedy. In terms of the range of measures that we're taking to protect young drivers, they include penalties for driving uninsured and unlicensed, and measures to reduce the risks posed by unroadworthy vehicles. And in terms of influence of her and her constituents, I'd be very happy to set up an appropriate meeting for her constituent.

He's right to remind us of what was a terrible scandal and I will ask the Water Minister to meet him and his constituents to discuss it. He and the public are right to be furious that companies are still polluting our seas, lakes and rivers. Mr. Speaker, we've taken action banning bonuses for bosses in six polluting companies, changing the law so that those who hide sewage spills can be locked up, and issuing almost 30 million pounds in fines to clean up waterways. We're clearing up the mess that the party over there left, like everything else.

Apparently the leader of Reform is in the lounge. I know he likes an early getaway at Christmas to get to his place in France. But Mr. Speaker, he lobbied for economic sanctions against his own country when he was in the United States, with no thought for British workers and zero patriotism. The difference is our US deal secured the best deal for the car industry, providing certainty for the workforce at JLR. And there's more good news, Mr. Speaker, for the car industry this week because Nissan is now building its new electric Leaf in Sunderland. That's the difference a Labour government makes.

Mr. Speaker, it is an important sector. At the heart of this challenge is the end of the temporary relief that was put in place during COVID, and that's why we put in place the transitional measures and investing half a million into our hospitality support scheme to help rural pubs diversify. On issues like the cost of living, we've taken a number of measures to make it easier for people to go out and enjoy themselves in pubs, and we'll always look at what measures we can put in place to support pubs.

Well, Mr. Speaker, the hub means more regular services for up to 15 stations across the region. That's vital after the Lichfield to Birmingham service was slashed under the previous government. The construction will create around 13,000 jobs and we're delivering them as quickly as possible with Network Rail awarding design contracts this week. Mr. Speaker, we're also freezing rail fares, that's the first time that that's happened in 30 years, saving his constituents about 90 pounds a year on the commute to Birmingham.

Happy Christmas. I saw that the honorable member was asking the public to suggest questions for today. I actually put in a bid, Mr. Speaker, I filled it in. I assume he missed the question I assumed. I said he should ask about the 6,000 well-paid high-skilled jobs we've secured in his constituency, building Typhoons thanks to an 8 billion deal with Turkey. I'm disappointed that he didn't want to talk about good well-paid jobs in his constituency secured by this Labour government.

Well, it is deeply concerning to hear about the closure of eight Derbyshire care homes by the Reform-led Derbyshire Council. It will be hugely concerning to residents and to their families. While we're making 3.7 billion pounds of extra funding available to councils to fund social care. And let me say to the member for Clacton relaxing in the lounge: Christmas is a time for forgiveness, it's never too late to apologize to former classmate.

Mr. Speaker, we had a mandate to change because we inherited major challenges across the country. If only he'd done something to solve these problems when he was working in Downing Street. He left a complete mess.

Mr. Speaker, we're replacing a failed settlement system with one that is fair and recognizes contribution. It is right to apply more stringent controls and we're currently consulting on the right approach. I do recognize the huge contribution of those working in our NHS and will not change the rules for those who already have settled status.

I thank him for raising this really important case and as he knows, we continually raise this with our counterparts and will continue to do so. And I condemn the conviction, obviously we await the sentence, but it's absolutely clear that he's been targeted by the authorities and this is wrongful and I call it out. It is important that we continue to engage so that we can raise this issue with those counterparts.

Can I thank him for raising this really important issue. The scale of violence and abuse suffered by women and girls is a national emergency, and the violence against women and girls strategy will be published tomorrow, setting out concrete steps in order to deal with this. We've already taken action to protect victims, including placing domestic abuse specialists in the first five 999 control rooms, and we're launching a new national policing center to coordinate police response and target these crimes. I'll make sure that ministers look specifically at issues that he's raised.
Well, as he will appreciate, there are rules and procedures in place in relation to hunger strikes and we're following those rules and procedures.

Yes is the simple answer to that question. And our decisions are already holding polluters to account. Mr. Speaker, new severe fines, banning bonuses and a record 83 criminal investigations have been launched. We've also secured over 100 billion pounds of investment to upgrade infrastructure to deliver better services to constituents.

Can I thank him for raising this and nobody could forget the shocking scenes at Lockerbie. And I know the huge impact it's had on the community that he grew up in, where people have responded with such compassion and strength. He has rightly stood by their search for justice and truth for all of the intervening years, and I pay tribute to that. All of our thoughts remain with the families and friends of all the victims who deserve truth, and I urge the Scottish authorities to consider the points that he raises.

Mr. Speaker, can I begin by saying I hope all colleagues had a happy Christmas. It probably feels quite a long time ago now, but not for reform, of course, because today is the day that they celebrate Christmas in Russia. Mr. Speaker, on Monday, I visited Reading, where I met with people who will benefit from the first freeze in rail fares for 30 years. Mr. Speaker, that's on top of other measures we've taken to tackle the cost of living. 150 pounds off energy bills, more free breakfast clubs, and raising the minimum wage. And there's much more to come this year, Mr. Speaker, as we turn the corner. Mr. Speaker, yesterday, I stood side by side with our European and American allies and President Zelensky at the Coalition of the Willing meeting in Paris. Mr. Speaker, we made real progress on security guarantees, which are vital for securing a just and lasting peace. Along with President Macron and President Zelensky, we agreed a declaration of intent on the deployment of forces in the event of a peace deal. Mr. Speaker, we will set out the details in a statement at the earliest opportunity. I will keep the House updated as the situation develops, and were troops to be deployed under the declaration signed, I would put that matter to the House for a vote. Mr. Speaker, this morning, I had meetings with ministerial colleagues and others. In addition to my duties in the House, I have further such meetings later today.

Well, I thank her for raising this important issue. We are taking serious action to deliver homes the country needs and provide homeowners with greater rights, powers, and protections. We will publish the draft bill as soon as possible, and I'll update the House. More protections, of course, are already coming this year because we passed the Renters' Rights Bill, strengthening protection for 9 million renters, abolishing no-fault evictions. That's the change we're delivering.

Mr. Speaker, let me be very clear about what was agreed yesterday because military plans were drawn up some months ago and I've updated the House in relation to that. Yesterday was a political declaration that sits under those military plans. If there were to be deployment, there would have to be a legal instrument. Mr. Speaker, deployment would only be after a ceasefire to support Ukraine's capabilities, to conduct deterrence operations and to construct and protect military hubs. Mr. Speaker, there will be a statement to the House at the earliest opportunity. There could hardly be an opportunity... they claim they want to know about this and they're trying to shout me down. Mr. Speaker, in relation to the House, if there were a decision to deploy under the agreement that was signed yesterday, then I would put that matter to this House for a debate beforehand and for a vote on that deployment. That is consistent with recent practice and I'll adhere to that.

Mr. Speaker, she says she wants to hear about Ukraine. She's got six questions, she's not even asking a second question about what we did yesterday. She's got the opportunity. Mr. Speaker, in relation... sorry, can I help the Prime Minister? You don't need to worry about the responsibility of the questions of the opposition, that's their job. Mr. Speaker, NATO is the single most important and effective military alliance the world has ever seen. In the 18 months we've been in power, I've done everything within my ability to strengthen NATO. We had one of the strongest NATO meetings last year, the summit, where we had more members of NATO and more unity. When I arrived back to the House to make a statement, which of course she asked for, her position was I shouldn't have missed PMQs, I should have empty-chaired the NATO summit. That's how serious she is about NATO, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I was with NATO allies yesterday, all day, in which we were discussing security in Europe, in particularly security guarantees for Ukraine and we made significant progress, and I'm glad that she has welcomed that. Of course I will speak to President Trump, I spoke to his senior advisors yesterday. We were with them, we were with them all day. But Mr. Speaker, Mr. Speaker, she asks me about the deployment. We released the statement yesterday. It's clear from that, but I will be clear with the House, that there would only be deployment after a ceasefire. It would be to support Ukraine's capabilities, to conduct deterrence operations and to construct and protect military hubs. The number will be determined in accordance with our military plans, which we are drawing up and looking to other members to support. So the number I will put before the House before we were to deploy, but I'll do more than that: if we went as far as a legal instrument to deploy, which would be necessary, I would then have a debate in this House so all members could know exactly what we're doing, make their points of view, and then we would have a vote in this House on the issue, which to my mind is the proper procedure in a situation such as this.

Mr. Speaker, just on this serious issue she puts to me in relation to security guarantees and the American role and our dialogue with the Americans, I can assure the House I spoke to President Trump twice over the Christmas period in relation to this specific issue, along with members of the E3, along with European allies. That has been a constant course of our discussion. There's no question of acting on this without full discussion with the Americans and their senior negotiators were there at President Trump's request yesterday and on his instructions and they were talking to him during the course of yesterday as we negotiated. So to reassure the House, because it is a serious position she's put to me on the question of security guarantees, there is nothing between the UK and the US and we've been constantly discussing this over many, many weeks and months. We've made huge progress. I have personally spoken to President Trump about it on two occasions since we were last in this House. I do want to reassure her and the House in relation to that really important issue. In relation to defense spend, I'm proud that we're investing to keep our country safe. That we have increased the defense spend, that's provided for in the budget. It's the biggest sustained increase in defense spending since the Cold War and that means, Mr. Speaker, better kit, better housing for our forces and better defense as an engine for growth. Mr. Speaker, that does compare to their record. Ben Wallace, who was on the radio this morning, the longest serving Conservative defense secretary, admitted that on their watch the armed services had been, in his words, hollowed out.

Mr. Speaker, they shout shame, I'll pass that on to Ben Wallace. Mr. Speaker, the defense spending that we've put in place is three years earlier than the unfunded plan that they left behind at the last election.

Mr. Speaker, that was embarrassing. She said that Ben Wallace was talking about all governments. They were in power for 14 years and they hollowed out our armed forces. Copyright Ben Wallace. Secondly, she's talked about the Shadow Cabinet. She has in her shadow cabinet a Shadow Attorney General who is advising Abramovich at the same time as we are imposing sanctions on Russia and trying to use that money to support Ukraine. How can someone sit in her shadow cabinet advising someone trying to escape sanctions and pretend that their policy is to support us on sanctions? And Mr. Speaker, Mr. Speaker, when it comes to Northern Ireland, they are the party... Mr. Robinson, wait, that gave immunity to IRA terrorists. Terrorists who killed British soldiers. Their flawed act was struck down by the courts, which left our veterans with no legal protection whatsoever. We're introducing a fair and transparent process with a package of rights and protections for our veterans. And Mr. Speaker, there is no equivalence between our armed forces who fought bravely in Northern Ireland and terrorist groups. And if the Leader of the Opposition wants to go back, if her position is, to their old flawed legislation and give immunity to the IRA, she should stand up now and say so.

Mr. Speaker, she talks about the Shadow Attorney General. Of course I accept that lawyers have to represent all sorts of clients. Of course I accept that principle. The question is whether the Shadow Attorney General can sit in the Shadow Cabinet when the party opposite says it supports us on sanctions. We want the money from Chelsea Football Club to go to Ukraine. I'm not sure whether that's her position. If it is her position, presumably it's something they discuss in the Shadow Cabinet, advised by a Shadow Attorney General who is representing the very man whose money we want to send to Ukraine. If she can't see the conflict of interest in that, then she shows no judgment and no leadership at all. Same old. It's a new year, but the Leader of the Opposition has got absolutely nothing to offer the country. She is totally irrelevant. Nobody is listening to her. Mr. Speaker, this is the year when on this side we turn a corner, people benefit from the decisions we made, 150 pounds off energy bills, freezing rail fares, and lifting half a million children out of poverty. We're turning the corner and there's much more to come.

Well, can I thank him for that question? I know that he's working hard on this scheme. As he knows, land investigation works are currently taking place to help establish the final costs. The Road Minister is looking closely at the scheme alongside about 40 others. We will prioritize schemes that deliver faster journeys and unlock new homes and jobs.

Well, there's plenty of things that Jeffrey and I have agreed on and disagreed with over the years. But let me set out our position. It is our long-standing position that Maduro was not a legitimate president in Venezuela and so nobody, I think, sheds any tears at his removal. And what we need, what we were saying before the weekend and we say again, is there needs to be a peaceful transition to democracy in Venezuela. Now, the benchmark of all actions of all countries is, of course, international law, and it is for the US to justify its actions accordingly. My focus is on the defense and security of the United Kingdom. And yesterday, we were working with NATO allies, including the US, on security guarantees for Ukraine. And it's only with security guarantees that we'll have a just and lasting peace in Ukraine, which is vitally important for Ukraine, for Europe, and for the United Kingdom.

Mr. Speaker, let me be... the Greenland issue is obviously very, very important and I thank him for raising it. The future of Greenland is for Greenland and the Kingdom of Denmark. And for Greenland and the Kingdom of Denmark alone. And yesterday, people would have seen that I put out a statement to that effect along with fellow allies in Europe. And of course, NATO is hugely important, the single most effective and important military alliance the world has ever known. He keeps encouraging me to sort of tug away at parts of NATO and to choose between Europe and the US. That would be a strategic mistake for our country. And yesterday, we were working with our NATO allies, including the US, our NATO ally, on a just and lasting peace in Ukraine. That will not happen without security guarantees from the Coalition of the Willing backed by the United States. That's a vitally important issue and we made progress on that. And there won't be a just and lasting peace in Ukraine without those security guarantees, and not achieving a just and lasting peace in Ukraine is not in our national interest. And that's why I'm applying so much time and energy to seeking to get that outcome.

Well, can I thank her for her question. The Belfast Good Friday Agreement is one of the greatest achievements of the last Labour government, and it enshrined Northern Ireland's place in the United Kingdom and set out, as she well knows, I know, clear principles and processes under that framework. I'm aware of the Assembly and Executive Review Committee inquiry into institutional reform, but I can indicate that we're always happy to discuss any proposals for reform which would lead to a consensus.

Well, can I thank him for his question and I know how deeply he feels about these issues. The bill, as he knows, will put in place new measures designed specifically to protect veterans. The safeguards have been developed with veterans in mind after carefully listening to their concerns. They have no respect at all, have they, for this issue. We've been meeting with veterans' organizations and listening to their views, and when the bill reaches the committee stages, the House will see the result of those considerations. You'll be pleased to hear that. We're determined to ensure protections are as fair and effective as possible, recognizing the role that service personnel played in keeping people across the UK safe during the Troubles, and I thank him for his question.

Can I thank her for raising that issue? As she knows, during COVID, the rates went down and that was coming to an end. And that's why we put in place interim relief as we move to the new rates. Mr. Speaker, we are continuing to work with and talk to the sector on that support and what further support and action we can take.

Can I thank her for raising this issue and assure her that we want to work with all colleagues across the House on this crucial issue and it's in our interest to do so. We did, as she said, launch the first ever Men's Health Strategy, announcing over 3.5 million pounds into supporting suicide prevention support programs, recruiting over 7,000 mental health workers including access to talking therapies, rolling out mental health support teams into schools. It is vital that we raise awareness and increase the support available, and I can assure her ministers would be happy to discuss her proposals with her because I genuinely want to work across the House on this really serious and tragic issue.

Well, Mr. Speaker, I'm very pleased about the measures we're about able to announce this week. Of course, that comes on top of the 5 million extra appointments that we've delivered in the first year of a Labour government and 300,000 taken off the waiting list, and more to come as we turn the year into 2026. But he's absolutely right. They laugh at the denial of the importance of vaccines. Imagine where this country would be if they ever saw power. And if you want an example of what it would be like, look at the local councils where they won power. They're absolutely chaotic, in a mess, and putting taxes up.

Mr. Speaker, I'll reflect on the fact that inflation is falling and the Bank of England says that it's going to be down to target. I'll reflect on the fact that we've had six interest rate cuts in a row. Mortgages... those with mortgages will be hugely effective. I'll reflect on the fact the IMF say we're going to have the second highest growth in 2025, defying the forecast. And I'd remind them that under them we had inflation at 11%, the worst parliament on living standards on record, and the Leader of the Opposition thinks that Liz Truss was 100% right to crash the economy. She's... they're literally the only people who think that anybody should be listening to them. Nobody is.

Can I thank her? And I speak for the whole House in saying I'm deeply sorry to hear about this tragic case and all of our thoughts are with the family. Obviously, there's a live legal case I can't comment on, but I can reassure her that we'll look closely at the final outcome of that case. There are strong rules in place, but we will look at the outcome of the case to see whether there's more that can be done.

Well, let me join her in paying tribute to the agencies and the local volunteers who supported the cleanup efforts. They're the very best. And I do pay tribute to them and join her in doing that. Liability sits with the polluter, and agencies and her local authority should work with responsible party to recover the costs. I will make sure that she gets the meeting that she has asked for with the appropriate minister.

Every mother and baby deserves safe, high-quality, compassionate care. And I want to see the inquiry at Leeds start as soon as possible. We're working with bereaved families to shape our approach and to appoint a chair who they can trust, as he knows. I have a huge amount of respect for Donna Ockenden. She's an outstanding advocate for families. We'll make sure that we select a chair of the highest standard who has the independence and expertise needed to deliver the real change that is needed.

Well, can I thank him and tell him alongside the record settlement that we've put in place for the Scottish Government, we're delivering huge investment in apprenticeships and offer a paid placement for every young person, which is vitally important. The SNP, on the other hand, blocked a welding facility in the Clyde because apparently it was related to defense. They don't back Scottish industry, young people, or national security. We do.

Yes, I do, Mr. Speaker. And I've been working with victims of violence against women and girls for the best part of 20 years, and I've assured them time and again that if we get the opportunity, we would make the system work better for them. They have to wait far too long for justice, and in many cases they don't see justice at all. I'm absolutely determined that we're going to turn that around.

We're not going to plow through farmland. We're going to make sensible proposals to build housing. Something they failed to do in 14 long years so young people now have not got the dream of homeownership because the inheritance we got from them. We're going to turn that around.

Mr. Speaker, can I start by condemning in the strongest possible terms the sickening repression and murder of protesters in Iran? The contrast between the courage of the Iranian people and the brutality of their desperate regime has never been clearer. Mr. Speaker, we've called out this brutality face-to-face, we're working with allies on further sanctions and doing all we can to protect UK nationals. Mr. Speaker, time and again under the party opposite, towns and cities across the North were failed. Today, this Labour government delivers change: a major new rail network across the North and a new Northern growth strategy. That is the renewal that this country voted for. This morning, I had meetings with ministerial colleagues and others, in addition to my duties in this House, I shall have further such meetings later today.

Can I start by thanking him for raising this case because it is very serious, very concerning. And all members of Parliament should be able to visit anywhere in their constituency, schools or other places, without any fear of antisemitism. We do take this seriously, we're providing more funding for security and support we're putting in across the country, and we will be holding those to account who prevented this visit to this school.

Can I thank my honorable friend? The Hillsborough Law will right wrongs of the past, changing the balance of power to ensure the state can never hide from the people it should serve. And I would like to acknowledge, Mr. Speaker, I think some of the families are in the gallery with us here today, and I will be meeting them later on this afternoon. I've always been clear the duty of candor applies to the intelligence services. I made a commitment we wouldn't water down the bill, and the amendments we put forward strengthen it. It is right that there are essential safeguards in place to protect national security, and we've got that balance right. I will meet the families and will outline the next steps on Monday in relation to that crucial balance.

Mr. Speaker, I'm determined to make it harder for people to work illegally in this country. And that's why there will be checks, they will be digital, and they will be mandatory. And I'll tell her what this government is doing. Whether on planning, child poverty, employment rights, investing in our NHS, we're taking the right choices for Britain, and they oppose every single one of them. And she talks about U-turns and consistency. From the party that used to recognize the challenge of climate change, and now they run from it. Who promised to cut immigration, but then lost control of it. Who once took great pride in our diversity, now they talk of deporting our neighbors to achieve cultural coherence. And Mr. Speaker, on consistency, don't get me started on five Prime Ministers, six Chancellors, eight Home Secretaries, sixteen Housing Ministers. They had more positions in 14 years than the Kama Sutra. No wonder they're knackered, and they left the country screwed.

Mr. Speaker, the principle we put in place on inheritance tax is the right one. We listened, we made an adjustment. But what we're doing is turning the country around. Yes, we've changed the country. We've changed the failed approach of the last Tory government. They crashed the economy and sent mortgage rates through the roof. They left millions stuck on NHS waiting lists. They presided over the worst parliament for living standards on record. Now we're turning that around, we're changing that. Inflation and interest rates are coming down, waiting lists are coming down, wages are up more in the first year of a Labour government than 10 years of the Tory government. But I understand, Mr. Speaker, that she's taking advice on change. She had Nadhim Zahawi in to ask his advice, how to change and how to save her party. Please don't tell me she listened to his accountant. The next day after the advice, he jumped ship to Reform, the 23rd former Tory MP to do so. I don't know which is more pitiful, the flood of former Tory MPs deserting her sinking ship, or the Reform party so desperate to launder any old failed Tory politician.

Mr. Speaker, we're working with the sector to ensure that they get the support that they need. I have to say, the leader of the opposition's newfound concern for pubs will come as a surprise to anyone who remembers the 7,000 pubs that were closed under the Tories. And as Business Secretary, she didn't say a word about it. So we support business, we also support workers, Mr. Speaker. And that's why we've passed our Employment Rights Act. And on Monday, the Business Secretary and I went to Croydon to discuss our Employment Rights Act with workers there. They were very keen on the paternity rights and the maternity rights, which I know the leader of the opposition opposes. And whilst we were there at IKEA, they showed me their new prototype, the IKEA shadow cabinet. The trouble is, nobody wants to buy it, it's mainly constructed of old dead wood, and every time you lose a nut, it defects to Reform.

Mr. Speaker, we're working with this sector. She hasn't explained why she said nothing about the 7,000 pubs that closed on her watch. We're doing other things on the cost of living to help people, to make sure they can get out to spend money in pubs and hospitality: boosting the minimum wage—what did they do? They opposed it. Freezing rail fares and prescription charges—what did they do? They opposed it. £150 off energy bills—what did they do? They opposed it. She said nothing when pubs were closing and she opposes every measure now. And she said a moment ago, 'I'm all right.' She clearly didn't listen to the advice of Nadhim Zahawi because what he told her he's now made public. He told her that they failed on mass migration, they failed on our armed forces, and he told her that she's leading, his words, 'a defunct brand the nation can no longer trust.' No wonder he's joined the Tory migration to Reform, Mr. Speaker. It's the second Boris wave.

Mr. Speaker, they crashed the economy and now they want to give lectures. She's wondering why nobody's listening to—nobody is ever going to listen to them on the economy ever again. Mr. Speaker, in 18 months because of the decisions we've made, inflation is falling and the Bank of England says it's coming back down to target. We've had six interest rate cuts in a row. Wages are up more in the first year of a Labour government than under the first 10 years of their government. And we've beat the forecast on growth for 2025. We're turning this country around after the appalling mess that they left it in.

Mr. Speaker, here's the difference. I changed my party, and that's why we stand here with a majority Labour government. She sits there with her party, her party that lost two-thirds of their MPs at the last election. And she's losing more every week. They're queuing up to join the member for Clacton's laundry service for disgraced Tory politicians. Meanwhile, inflation is down, wages are up, and waiting lists are down. Labour's turning the corner and changing this country for the better.

She draws attention to the important work of the Mayor of London, and nobody should be talking our country down or talking London down. And she's right to say that since we came into office, the number of knife crime offenses is down. But Mr. Speaker, there is more to do. We're introducing new powers to seize knives and increasing the penalty for selling knives to under-18s. And the party opposite, what did they do? They're chuntering. They voted against those provisions. And what's obvious about London and Reform is they've got a candidate for mayor who doesn't like London, a new Tory recruit who struggled to pay his taxes in this country, and a leader who spends more time in France than in his constituency.

Can I first say through him to Sandra that that's simply not acceptable for her or for anybody else, and I'd appreciate if he passes that on to her directly? We have put record investment into the NHS so we can turn this problem around, and we are turning it around. I would say to him that he puts forward his plans for change, but he never votes for the increase in investment and the measures that are needed to actually put that into practice. You can't change things without investing in them. You can't call for change and vote against a budget that puts a record investment into the NHS.

Can I thank him for raising this because the situation is clearly totally unacceptable. And he will want to know that Ministers have chaired daily emergency meetings to hold the company to account, to deliver on the change that's urgently needed at the moment in all the areas that he mentioned. We've also doubled the compensation rates for individuals and businesses, and we're absolutely clear the company must urgently invest in infrastructure. And we'll publish the Water White Paper in due course, but we are holding those daily meetings to hold this company to account.

Can I pay tribute to her as a dedicated campaigner on this and so many other issues? And I'm delighted that today we're announcing a transformation in journeys across the North. Of course, it was said and promised many times by the party opposite, but never delivered. We're taking action and delivering. We're working with Kirklees Council to prepare the business case for the first phase of upgrading the line, and I know the Transport Secretary would be happy to discuss the details of that with her.

Can I thank him for raising this and tell him I spoke to the Taoiseach in December about this, and I know he's committed to delivering on this? The new legacy unit has been established within the Garda, and I'm confident the Irish government's other commitments will be delivered as set out in the joint framework. For the first time, information held by the Irish authorities is being shared with a reformed Legacy Commission, meaning more families and victims of terrorism getting information about what happened to their loved ones.

Can I sound very proud of what we're doing on child poverty, lifting half a million children out of poverty? The party opposite says their policy is to plunge them straight back into poverty, and they should be ashamed of that. The situation she draws my attention to is appalling. Parents and teachers are furious that the party opposite left schools literally crumbling. We've invested, Mr. Speaker, £20 billion to rebuild around 800 schools, and our aim is all schools and colleges in England that aren't being fully or substantially rebuilt to be RAAC-free by the end of the Parliament, and I'll make sure a Minister meets with her to discuss this.

I thank him for raising this and he knows we inherited a terrible situation with waiting lists, performance targets missed, and hospitals like Stepping Hill left to crumble. They should be absolutely ashamed of themselves. I'm pleased the new outpatients building is open, and because of our decisions, the local Trust will receive £75 million in capital funding. Progress is being made. His local Trust has seen waiting lists fall by almost 3,000, the number of waits over a year is down by 67%. I will make sure he gets the meeting that he wants to discuss the details further.

Can I thank her for raising this? The actions of grope and X are disgusting and they're shameful. And frankly, the decision to then turn this into a premium service is horrific. And we're absolutely determined to take action here. We've made it clear that X has to act, and if not, Ofcom has our full backing and we'll introduce and are introducing legislation. Mr. Speaker, to update the House, I have been informed this morning that X is acting to ensure full compliance with UK law. If so, that is welcome, but we're not going to back down. They must act, we will take the necessary measures, we will strengthen existing laws and prepare for legislation if it needs to go further, and Ofcom will continue its independent investigation.

Can I thank her for raising this, and it's astonishing that Reform defend Musk on this issue. It is complete—I said the images are disgusting, their position is disgusting on this. This is weaponizing images of women and children that should never be made. And that's why we're acting. Reform not only—Reform refused to do anything about it. But more than that, the point she raises is really—they would scrap the Online Safety Act that stops children accessing content like pornography, suicide, self-harm, and eating disorders. They're an absolute disgrace and know nothing about protecting children.

Mr. Speaker, this is a question of values and freedom. And I'm proud of the British workers in his constituency, in fact, supporting our Ukrainian allies. Ukrainian soldiers are defending European values on the front line every day. And Mr. Speaker, in the event of a ceasefire, a multinational force will carry out defense and deterrence operations and conduct training, planning, recovery, and regeneration of Ukrainian forces. But this week the leader of Reform said Russia had a 'casus belli.' That—that means—that means a justification for war in invading Ukraine. A Putin apologist using Russia's talking points.

Diego Garcia is a vital military base with important capabilities for our own. It's integral to our security. Our decision was welcomed by our allies, the Five Eyes, India, and the United States. It was opposed by our—our enemies, including Russia. Now we can add the Tories to that list and Reform to that list. The Tories following Reform, Reform following Putin.

Could I just say that my thoughts and I think the thoughts of the whole House will be with all those affected by the terrible road traffic accident in her constituency over the weekend and our thoughts with all of those so awfully impacted? On her question, we are determined to restore the dream of homeownership. That's why there's been £39 billion of investment to deliver the biggest boost in social and affordable housing in a generation. Through planning reforms, the New Homes Accelerator, and new towns, we're determined to deliver the homes that people need.

Can I thank him for his support on what we're doing on violence against women and girls? Can I also agree with him that this isn't about women or men or boys or girls? It's about both. And that's why I was very pleased to bring forward our men's health strategy, one of the first of its sort, to deal with the challenges that young men in particular, in my view, have growing up, particularly with social media, but also to go further on the question of suicide, and I know that that's something that the whole House is prepared to work together on and quite right too.

Can I thank her for raising that because the Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo is absolutely brilliant, as anybody who's seen it will attest? And I'm so pleased that it's heading to New Zealand. And I think it's another example of Scotland's unique contribution to our international image, our culture, and tourism. And I think we all wish them the very best of luck in their performance, and I know it'll be very well received.

I disagree as he knows with the decision of the West Midlands Police, and the Home Secretary will be making a statement in relation to it today. Mr. Speaker, the Home Secretary used to have power to remove chief constables. That power was stripped by the 2011 Police Reform Act. The honorable member knows who was making decisions in the Home Office at the time; it was him working for Theresa May that stripped that power away.

Can I thank her for raising the case of Clover? NHS England and the National Institute of Health and Care Research recently agreed funding for two world-first clinical trials relating to use of cannabis-based products. This could help see medicines more routinely available in the NHS, and I'll make sure that she gets the meeting that she wants with the relevant Minister to discuss what else we're doing.

Can I credit her with helping expose this scandal and working with her and everyone in her community volunteering to clean up the beaches? That is the very best of who we are. But people are right to be furious that for far too long water companies were allowed to get away with polluting our seas and beaches. The Environment Agency are leading a full investigation, but we are more generally ending unfair bonuses for polluting water bosses, abolishing Ofwat, and introducing tougher penalties, holding companies to account.

I will join him and thank the staff in his hospital but also the NHS staff—NHS staff across the country who worked so hard over Christmas and New Year, which is notoriously a difficult time. And that completes Prime Minister's Questions. Let the front benches change over.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. In recent days, I've spoken extensively to our international allies, including European leaders and others, the US and NATO. We will continue to engage constructively to resolve issues, particularly relating to international security, applying the principles and values that I set out on Monday. Mr. Speaker, in addition this week, the government has announced a landmark investment to support children with special educational needs, overhauled our water system, and today launched a £15 billion plan to create warm homes. At home and abroad, this Labour government is delivering for the British people. This morning I had meetings with ministerial colleagues and others. In addition to my duties in this house, I shall have further such meetings later today.

Can I thank my honorable friend? I know how much he cares about making life affordable. Mr. Speaker, we're taking £150 off energy bills, that's £300 for the six million poorest families, including almost 3,700 households in his constituency. The warm homes plan we're announcing today is the biggest ever public investment in upgrading British homes. It will lift one million households out of fuel poverty, tackling the cost of living. That's the difference a Labour government makes.

Well, Mr. Speaker, engaging constructively on international security matters hugely, particularly when it comes to security in the Arctic, and that's the context in which this discussion is going on in relation to Greenland. As we engage constructively, I have made my position clear on our principles and values. The first of those is that the future of Greenland is for the people of Greenland and the Kingdom of Denmark alone. The second is that threats of tariffs to pressurize allies are completely wrong. Mr. Speaker, we will continue to engage constructively. I've had many international calls in recent days, and the Prime Minister of Denmark is coming to the United Kingdom tomorrow for bilateral talks. But I do want to be clear with the house: I will not yield, Britain will not yield on our principles and values about the future of Greenland under threats of tariffs. And that is my clear position.

Mr. Speaker, I've made out my position on Greenland absolutely clear on Monday and a moment ago. President Trump deployed words on Chagos yesterday that were different to his previous words of welcome and support when I met him in the White House. He deployed those words yesterday for the express purpose of putting pressure on me and Britain in relation to my values and principles on the future of Greenland. Mr. Speaker, he wants me to yield on my position, and I'm not going to do so. Given that that was his express purpose, I'm surprised the Leader of the Opposition has jumped on the bandwagon. I had understood her position to be that she supported the government's position on the future of Greenland. Now she appears to support words by President Trump to undermine the government's position on the future of Greenland. She's chosen naked opportunism over the national interest.
